title: The Long and Short of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
research_question: What are the short-run adjustment costs and long-run efficiency gains from a reciprocal trade liberalization between two industrialized economies? Specifically, how do reciprocal tariff reductions affect employment, labor productivity, earnings, wages, skill composition, import prices, and trade creation/diversion in the liberalizing country?
data_description: The study uses Canadian data from the Annual Survey of Manufactures (ASM), the Canadian Labour Force Survey, and Statistics Canada's International Trade, Input-Output, Prices, and Standards Divisions, including special tabulations of plant-level (long-form) records. U.S. data come primarily from the NBER Manufacturing Productivity Database and Feenstra's trade data, updated through 1996; comparison data for Japan and the U.K. come from UNIDO. The unit of observation is the 4-digit Canadian SIC industry (213 manufacturing industries) and continuing manufacturing plants (3,801 plants present in 1980, 1986, 1988, and 1996). Key variables include nominal and effective tariff rates (Canadian against U.S. and U.S. against Canadian, constructed from tariff-line duties/imports), employment of production and nonproduction workers, earnings, hourly wages, hours, output, value added, labor productivity, plant age, and HS10 import prices and quantities. The pre-policy period is 1980–1986 and the policy period is 1988–1996.
institutional_context: The setting is the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA), implemented on January 1, 1989, which mandated reciprocal annual tariff reductions between Canada and the United States while leaving tariffs against the rest of the world unchanged. In 1988, Canada's average manufacturing tariff against the U.S. was 8.1 percent (effective rate 16 percent), with roughly one in four 4-digit Canadian industries sheltered by tariffs above 10 percent—typically low-wage, low-capital, low-margin industries. The corresponding U.S. tariff against Canada averaged 4 percent. The agreement was a clean policy shock for an industrialized economy: tariff cuts were not bundled with broader market reforms or triggered by macroeconomic crises, unlike most developing-country liberalizations. Tariff concessions were phased in linearly, generally over five or ten years, and varied substantially across narrowly defined industries, generating sharp cross-industry variation in exposure to import competition and export-market access.
